questions.question: A system must read a source sequence and generate a related output sequence. Which architecture matches that task?
options: A bidirectional encoder alone
A decoder-only next-token model
A convolutional image classifier
An encoder-decoder transformer
questions.explanation: Encoder-decoder models encode the input once, then autoregressively generate a related output while cross-attending to that source representation. An encoder alone produces representations but has no decoder to emit the target sequence.

questions.question: In T5 span corruption, what does the decoder target contain?
options: Only the uncorrupted tokens from the source sequence
A class label for every masked position in sequence
The complete clean source sentence, including unmasked tokens
Sentinel markers followed by the removed source text spans
questions.explanation: T5 replaces each selected input span with a sentinel and trains the decoder to emit the sentinels followed by only the removed text. Returning every uncorrupted token would reconstruct the full source instead of the span-corruption target.

questions.question: How does BART’s denoising target differ from T5’s span-corruption target?
options: BART predicts the next sentence label only
BART predicts only the masked spans
BART outputs a speaker or source identifier
BART reconstructs the original full sequence
questions.explanation: BART applies noise to the input and trains its decoder to reconstruct the complete original sequence. T5’s target contains only corrupted spans, so the full-sequence BART objective asks the decoder to produce more output tokens.

questions.question: During autoregressive decoding, what happens to the encoder output after it is computed?
options: It becomes the decoder’s next-token label sequence
It is reused at each decoder step for cross-attention
It is recomputed from the growing target each step
It is discarded after the first output token
questions.explanation: The encoder processes the source once; each autoregressive decoder step reuses that same encoded output as keys and values for cross-attention. Recomputing it from the growing target would repeat source work without changing the source representation.

questions.question: A speech recognizer maps audio features to text tokens. Which architecture does the lesson cite as a natural fit?
options: A patch classifier with one output per image
An encoder-decoder model such as Whisper
An encoder-only model with a sentence label
A decoder-only model with no source representation
questions.explanation: Whisper is the lesson’s example of an encoder-decoder mapping from audio input to text output: the encoder represents the audio while the decoder generates transcript tokens. A sentence-label encoder does not produce a transcript.

questions.question: A translation task has a narrow output distribution. Which decoding strategy does the lesson call standard?
options: Greedy decoding with no candidate comparison
High-temperature sampling with a broad distribution
Beam search with width around four or five
Random sampling from the source vocabulary
questions.explanation: Translation has a relatively narrow output distribution, so the lesson calls beam search with width four or five standard: it compares several partial sequences. High-temperature sampling favors variety rather than the best-scoring candidate sequence.
